PHSCS 587

MOSFET terminal capacitance

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how intrinsic gate coupling changes between low-drain-bias inversion and saturation

A MOSFET is a multi-terminal device. Its small-signal capacitances come from derivatives of terminal charge with respect to terminal voltage under a stated sign convention and fixed remaining biases. A single oxide capacitance does not describe every terminal response.

For an ideal long-channel transistor in strong inversion at very low VDS, symmetry gives intrinsic Cgs ≈ Cgd ≈ CₒₓWL/2. In saturation, the channel charge model gives Cgs ≈ 2CₒₓWL/3 and intrinsic Cgd ≈ 0. The gate-to-body channel contribution is small in these strong-inversion limits.

These are limiting quasi-static results, not a complete high-frequency capacitance matrix. Source/drain overlap, fringing, junction capacitance and non-quasi-static transport add further terms. A near-zero intrinsic Cgd does not mean an actual device has zero drain-to-gate coupling.

Example

If the oxide area capacitance is 8 fF/μm² and WL = 0.50 μm², CₒₓWL = 4 fF. The ideal low-VDS intrinsic Cgs and Cgd are about 2 fF each; the saturation Cgs is about 2.67 fF before extrinsic contributions.

Sources and scope

Practice

1. Why is the saturation limit Cgd ≈ 0 insufficient for predicting switching feedback in a real circuit?

List capacitances intentionally excluded from the intrinsic model.

Overlap and fringing capacitances still couple gate and drain, and bias-dependent/non-quasi-static effects can matter. The intrinsic limiting value is only one contribution.
